rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> laboratory soil-column experiment with a transient flow apparatus on two repacked soils at several bulk densities, with subsurface drip irrigation (350 mL) and aeration (1050 mL) through the emitter. Q2: Results, 'Impact of Aeration following Drip Irrigation on Soil Air Permeability' and Fig. 6 <U+2013> air permeability within 10 min after aeration through the SDI emitter was 3.7, 2.0 and 1.5 times the pre-aeration level for the Brown Forest soil at bulk densities 1.3, 1.4, 1.5 g cm-3 and 3.0, 2.5, 2.0 times for the Lou soil; average post-aeration permeability was about 70% (Brown Forest) and 88% (Lou) of pre-irrigation, versus 54.8% and 67.6% at 24 h without aeration. Q8: Discussion and Conclusions <U+2013> authors note that disturbed, repacked samples were used so soil structure may have been destroyed (offered to explain a contradiction with Schj<U+00F8>nning et al. 1999), and that further experiments with undisturbed structured soils are needed.
rows.notes: Single measurement method (transient air permeability via manometer pressure decay); the comparison of classical vs modified apparatus is a calibration of instruments, not independent triangulation of the aeration effect. The mechanism (air forcing water redistribution and restoring pore continuity) is asserted ('probably'), not measured <U+2013> soil water content was not reported. Only two soils, laboratory columns, no field or larger scale. Texture and bulk density are reported as factors the effect varied with, not stated as requirements. No standard deviations, ranges or confidence intervals are given for the air permeability results; only R2 of regression fits.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a laboratory soil-column experiment on air permeability after subsurface drip irrigation and after forced aeration through the SDI emitter; it supports the air-permeability part of the claim but does not address soil mechanical strength or air-filled porosity directly.
